LANGUAGE plpgsql

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_tier   varchar(20);
    v_status varchar(20);
    rec      record;
BEGIN
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    FOR rec IN
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count

        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name

            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,

    END LOOP;

    SELECT status INTO v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;

- CALL outside an explicit transaction: procedure runs in its own transaction, and COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside end that transaction and start a new one.
- CALL inside an explicit transaction block (BEGIN; ... CALL ...; COMMIT;): transaction control commands inside the procedure cause an error. Actually I believe the error is raised: "invalid transaction termination" SQLSTATE 2D000? Yes! CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    -- v_tier holds the computed loyalty tier for the current row.
    v_tier    varchar(20);
    -- Was anchored to customers.status in Oracle; anchored types are spelled
    -- out explicitly here (customers.status is varchar(20)).
    v_status  varchar(20);
    rec       record;
BEGIN
    -- Recompute from scratch, mirroring the Oracle procedure.
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    -- Cursor FOR loop over the per-customer order aggregate. Active customers
    -- only (missing status counts as active, as in the original). Rows are
    -- produced lowest spend first so the result set is deterministic.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name
        ORDER BY total_spend, customer_id
    ) LOOP
        IF rec.total_spend >= 1000 THEN
            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        INSERT INTO customer_tiers
            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original fetched one arbitrary customer status into a variable;
    -- the Oracle row-limiting predicate becomes LIMIT 1 here.
    SELECT status INTO v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;
$proc$;

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    -- Row buffer for the report table; the Oracle declaration was anchored to
    -- the table's row shape, which in plpgsql is simply the table's row type.
    v_row       monthly_report;
    v_has_data  numeric := 0;
    rec         record;
    -- The Oracle procedure declared a named exception; PostgreSQL has no
    -- DECLARE ... EXCEPTION, so the name is kept as a condition code that
    -- RAISE and the handler below both refer to.
    e_no_data   constant text := 'no_data_found';
BEGIN
    -- The original counted the Oracle one-row dummy table, which always
    -- yields 1; a SELECT with no FROM does the same in PostgreSQL.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

    -- Aggregate order_items by product category. Highest revenue first so the
    -- result set is deterministic.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT p.category                                   AS category,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
        FROM   order_items oi
        JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
        GROUP  BY p.category
        ORDER BY revenue DESC, category
    ) LOOP
        v_row.report_month := p_month;
        v_row.category     := rec.category;
        v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
        v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

        INSERT INTO monthly_report
            (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
        VALUES
            (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
    END LOOP;

    IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for monthly report'
            USING ERRCODE = e_no_data;
    END IF;
EXCEPTION
    WHEN no_data_found THEN
        -- Matches the Oracle handler for the named exception: the work done
        -- by this procedure is rolled back (the exception block discards
        -- changes made inside it) and the error is not re-raised.
        NULL;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        -- Unexpected error: undo this procedure's work and bubble the error up.
        RAISE;
END;
$proc$;

-- ============================================================================
-- PostgreSQL plpgsql conversions of the two Oracle stored procedures in
-- oracle/sp_customer_tier.sql and oracle/sp_monthly_report.sql.
--
-- Oracle construct -> PostgreSQL equivalent used here:
--   * implicit cursor FOR loop          -> FOR ... IN (SELECT ...) LOOP
--   * Oracle null-substitution call     -> COALESCE(...)
--   * Oracle current-server-time call   -> now()
--   * first-locked-row fetch            -> ... LIMIT 1
--   * variable anchored to a column     -> the column's type spelled out
--   * variable anchored to a table row  -> the table's row type
--   * Oracle one-row dummy table        -> SELECT with no FROM (one implicit row)
--   * named user-defined exception      -> RAISE ... USING ERRCODE plus a
--                                          matching WHEN arm in the handler
--   * COMMIT / ROLLBACK inside the procedures were dropped: a PostgreSQL
--     procedure runs inside the caller's transaction, and the plpgsql
--     exception block already undoes this procedure's own work on error.
-- ============================================================================

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Procedure 1: sp_customer_tier
-- Recomputes the lifetime tier of every ACTIVE customer from their orders.
-- GOLD for a lifetime spend of at least 1000, SILVER for at least 500,
-- otherwise BRONZE. Writes one aggregate row per customer into
-- customer_tiers.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_tier    varchar(20);
    v_status  varchar(20);   -- same type as customers.status
    rec       record;
BEGIN
    -- Recompute from scratch, exactly like the original.
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    -- Row-by-row pass over the per-customer order aggregate. A customer with
    -- no status counts as ACTIVE. ORDER BY keeps the insert order (and hence
    -- the table's row order) deterministic, lowest spend first.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name
        ORDER BY total_spend, customer_id
    ) LOOP
        IF rec.total_spend >= 1000 THEN
            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        INSERT INTO customer_tiers
            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original read one arbitrary customer status into a local variable
    -- (a single-row fetch); LIMIT 1 is the PostgreSQL spelling of that.
    SELECT status INTO v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;
$proc$;

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Procedure 2: sp_monthly_report(p_month)
-- Rebuilds the revenue report for one month: aggregates order_items by
-- product category into monthly_report. Mirrors the original's named
-- exception and exception handler.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_row       monthly_report;    -- row buffer: the report table's row type
    v_has_data  numeric := 0;
    rec         record;
    -- PostgreSQL has no DECLARE ... EXCEPTION, so the Oracle exception name is
    -- kept as the error condition its RAISE and handler below both use.
    e_no_data   constant text := 'no_data_found';
BEGIN
    -- The original counted a guaranteed single dummy row, so v_has_data is
    -- always 1 here too: a SELECT without FROM evaluates against exactly one
    -- implicit row in PostgreSQL.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

    -- Aggregate order_items by product category; missing sums become 0.
    -- Highest revenue first keeps the insert order deterministic.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT p.category                                   AS category,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
        FROM   order_items oi
        JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
        GROUP  BY p.category
        ORDER BY revenue DESC, category
    ) LOOP
        v_row.report_month := p_month;
        v_row.category     := rec.category;
        v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
        v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

        INSERT INTO monthly_report
            (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
        VALUES
            (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
    END LOOP;

    IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for monthly report'
            USING ERRCODE = e_no_data;
    END IF;
EXCEPTION
    WHEN no_data_found THEN
        -- Same shape as the Oracle handler for its named exception: the work
        -- done inside this block is rolled back and the error is swallowed.
        NULL;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        -- Unexpected failure: undo this procedure's work and re-throw.
        RAISE;
END;
$proc$;

-- ============================================================================
-- PostgreSQL plpgsql conversions of the two Oracle stored procedures from
-- oracle/sp_customer_tier.sql and oracle/sp_monthly_report.sql.
--
-- Oracle construct -> PostgreSQL equivalent used below:
--   * implicit cursor FOR loop           -> FOR ... IN (SELECT ...) LOOP
--   * Oracle null-substitution call      -> COALESCE(...)
--   * Oracle current-server-time call    -> now()
--   * Oracle single-row fetch idiom      -> ... LIMIT 1
--   * variable anchored to a column      -> the column's type, spelled out
--   * variable anchored to a table row   -> the table's row type
--   * Oracle one-row dummy table         -> SELECT with no FROM (one implicit row)
--   * named user-defined exception       -> RAISE ... USING ERRCODE plus a
--                                           matching WHEN arm in the handler
--   * COMMIT / ROLLBACK inside procedures were dropped: a PostgreSQL procedure
--     runs inside the caller's transaction, and the plpgsql exception block
--     already undoes this procedure's own work when an error is caught.
-- ============================================================================

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- sp_customer_tier: recompute the lifetime tier of every ACTIVE customer from
-- their orders (GOLD for a lifetime spend of at least 1000, SILVER for at
-- least 500, otherwise BRONZE) and write one aggregate row per customer into
-- customer_tiers.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_tier    varchar(20);
    v_status  varchar(20);              -- same type as customers.status
    rec       record;
BEGIN
    -- Recompute from scratch, exactly like the original.
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    -- Row-by-row pass over the per-customer order aggregate. A customer with
    -- no status counts as ACTIVE. The ORDER BY keeps the insert order (and
    -- therefore the table's row order) deterministic, lowest spend first.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name
        ORDER BY total_spend, customer_id
    ) LOOP
        IF rec.total_spend >= 1000 THEN
            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        INSERT INTO customer_tiers
            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original also fetched one arbitrary customer status into a local
    -- variable; LIMIT 1 is the PostgreSQL spelling of that single-row fetch.
    SELECT status INTO v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;
$proc$;

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- sp_monthly_report(p_month): rebuild the revenue report for one month by
-- aggregating order_items per product category into monthly_report. Keeps the
-- original's named exception and exception handler.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_row       monthly_report;         -- row buffer: the report table's row type
    v_has_data  numeric := 0;
    rec         record;
    -- PostgreSQL has no DECLARE ... EXCEPTION clause, so the Oracle exception
    -- name survives as the error condition that both the RAISE below and the
    -- handler at the end refer to.
    e_no_data   constant text := 'no_data_found';
BEGIN
    -- The original counted a guaranteed single dummy row, which always yields
    -- 1; a SELECT with no FROM evaluates against exactly one implicit row in
    -- PostgreSQL, so v_has_data behaves identically here.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

    -- Aggregate order_items by product category; missing sums become 0.
    -- Highest revenue first keeps the insert order deterministic.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT p.category                                   AS category,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
        FROM   order_items oi
        JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
        GROUP  BY p.category
        ORDER BY revenue DESC, category
    ) LOOP
        v_row.report_month := p_month;
        v_row.category     := rec.category;
        v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
        v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

        INSERT INTO monthly_report
            (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
        VALUES
            (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
    END LOOP;

    IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for the monthly report'
            USING ERRCODE = e_no_data;
    END IF;
EXCEPTION
    WHEN no_data_found THEN
        -- Mirrors the Oracle handler for its named exception: the work done
        -- inside this block is rolled back and the error is not re-thrown.
        NULL;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        -- Unexpected failure: undo this procedure's work and re-throw.
        RAISE;
END;
$proc$;

--   * Oracle single-row fetch idiom     -> ... LIMIT 1
--   * variable anchored to a column     -> the column's type, spelled out
--   * variable anchored to a table row  -> the table's row type
--   * Oracle one-row dummy table        -> SELECT with no FROM (one implicit row)
--   * named user-defined exception      -> RAISE ... USING ERRCODE plus a
--                                          matching WHEN arm in the handler
--   * COMMIT / ROLLBACK inside procedures were dropped: a PostgreSQL procedure
--     runs inside the caller's transaction, and the plpgsql exception block
--     already undoes this procedure's own work when an error is caught.
-- ============================================================================

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- sp_customer_tier: recompute the lifetime tier of every ACTIVE customer from
-- their orders (GOLD for a lifetime spend of at least 1000, SILVER for at
-- least 500, otherwise BRONZE) and write one aggregate row per customer into
-- customer_tiers.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_customer_tier()
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_tier    varchar(20);
    v_status  varchar(20);              -- same type as customers.status
    rec       record;
BEGIN
    -- Recompute from scratch, exactly like the original.
    DELETE FROM customer_tiers;

    -- Row-by-row pass over the per-customer order aggregate. A customer with
    -- no status counts as ACTIVE. The ORDER BY keeps the insert order (and
    -- therefore the table's row order) deterministic, lowest spend first.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT o.customer_id,
               c.customer_name,
               SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spend,
               COUNT(*)           AS order_count
        FROM   orders o
        JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
        WHERE  COALESCE(c.status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE'
        GROUP  BY o.customer_id, c.customer_name
        ORDER BY total_spend, customer_id
    ) LOOP
        IF rec.total_spend >= 1000 THEN
            v_tier := 'GOLD';
        ELSIF rec.total_spend >= 500 THEN
            v_tier := 'SILVER';
        ELSE
            v_tier := 'BRONZE';
        END IF;

        INSERT INTO customer_tiers
            (customer_id, customer_name, total_spend, order_count, tier, computed_at)
        VALUES
            (rec.customer_id, rec.customer_name, rec.total_spend, rec.order_count,
             v_tier, now());
    END LOOP;

    -- The original also fetched one arbitrary customer status into a local
    -- variable; LIMIT 1 is the PostgreSQL spelling of that single-row fetch.
    SELECT status INTO v_status FROM customers LIMIT 1;
END;

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- sp_monthly_report(p_month): rebuild the revenue report for one month by
-- aggregating order_items per product category into monthly_report. Keeps the
-- original's named exception and exception handler.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_monthly_report(p_month varchar)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $proc$
DECLARE
    v_row       monthly_report;         -- row buffer: the report table's row type
    v_has_data  numeric := 0;
    rec         record;
    -- PostgreSQL has no DECLARE ... EXCEPTION clause, so the Oracle exception
    -- name survives as the error condition that both the RAISE below and the
    -- handler at the end refer to.
    e_no_data   constant text := 'no_data_found';
BEGIN
    -- The original counted a guaranteed single dummy row, which always yields
    -- 1; a SELECT with no FROM evaluates against exactly one implicit row in
    -- PostgreSQL, so v_has_data behaves identically here.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_has_data;

    DELETE FROM monthly_report WHERE report_month = p_month;

    -- Aggregate order_items by product category; missing sums become 0.
    -- Highest revenue first keeps the insert order deterministic.
    FOR rec IN (
        SELECT p.category                                   AS category,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue,
               COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0)                 AS units_sold
        FROM   order_items oi
        JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
        GROUP  BY p.category
        ORDER BY revenue DESC, category
    ) LOOP
        v_row.report_month := p_month;
        v_row.category     := rec.category;
        v_row.revenue      := rec.revenue;
        v_row.units_sold   := rec.units_sold;

        INSERT INTO monthly_report
            (report_month, category, revenue, units_sold)
        VALUES
            (v_row.report_month, v_row.category, v_row.revenue, v_row.units_sold);
    END LOOP;

    IF v_has_data = 0 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'no data available for the monthly report'
            USING ERRCODE = e_no_data;
    END IF;
EXCEPTION
    WHEN no_data_found THEN
        -- Mirrors the Oracle handler for its named exception: the work done
        -- inside this block is rolled back and the error is not re-thrown.
        NULL;
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        -- Unexpected failure: undo this procedure's work and re-throw.
        RAISE;
END;
$proc$;
